No open measured study of lock striping was found in this pass; the file gives only a textbook reference (Herlihy and Shavit ch. 13).
Lehman and Yao 1981 has no throughput figure: the paper says the efficiency gain could be quantified by simulation, and gives none.
The ART paper (Leis and others 2016) tests one writer and one reader, so no run has many writers on one structure; its throughput curves (Figure 5) are images, not text.
Bw-tree 2013 runs every test with 8 worker threads on 8 logical cores, and has no curve of throughput against writer count.
The Wang 2018 Bw-tree test used two Xeon E5-2680 v2 machines with 20 threads pinned to one socket.
No paper read in this pass plots throughput against the number of writers on one shared structure for all schemes.
Latch coupling on a B-tree was not measured in the ART paper, which covers lock coupling on a radix tree; Wang 2018 covers a B+tree with OLC.

claim: Wikipedia (Lock) summary: coarse-grained locks cost little but contend more, while fine-grained locks contend less but cost memory, time and deadlock risk.
McKenney perfbook 2023: a same-CPU compare-and-swap (CAS) consumes about seven nanoseconds, more than ten times the clock period.
McKenney perfbook 2023: a blind CAS between cores on the same socket consumes almost fifty nanoseconds, almost one hundred clock cycles.
McKenney perfbook 2023: a blind CAS with CPUs on different sockets consumes almost 150 nanoseconds, more than three hundred clock cycles.
McKenney 2001 (RCU paper): each lock acquisition writes the lock's data structure, so it is normally in the modified state only in the cache of the last acquiring CPU.
Lock failure modes, summary only: convoying, priority inversion and deadlock, with one global lock order as the fix.
McKenney perfbook 2023: reader-writer locking scalability is decidedly non-ideal, especially for smaller critical sections, because every acquiring thread must update the lock's data structure.
McKenney perfbook 2023 (448-CPU x86, 30 runs): reader-writer locking is more than an order of magnitude slower than RCU on one CPU and more than four orders of magnitude slower on 192 CPUs.
McKenney perfbook 2023: the reader-writer-lock gap is exaggerated by unrealistic zero-length critical sections.
note: The file adds, as its own gloss and not the book's words, that the RCU advantage shrinks as the critical section grows.

claim: Wikipedia (readers-writer lock) summary: read-preferring locks can starve writers, write-preferring locks cost concurrency, and upgrading from read to write by two readers deadlocks.
McKenney perfbook 2023: per-bucket locking partitions spacetime, so if the bucket count is large enough a CPU should with high probability get immediate access to a given bucket.

McKenney perfbook 2023, read-only hash test: RCU and hazard pointers scale much better than per-bucket locking, which in turn beats a globally locked table, because read-only replication avoids NUMA effects.
Striping failure modes, textbook per the file: a hot key sends all writers to one stripe, and resize and count take every lock.
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper): lock coupling performs very badly on modern multi-core CPUs even if the locks do not logically conflict, for example in read-only workloads.
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper): each read-lock acquisition, which writes to the node, invalidates all copies of that cache line in the other cores' caches.
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper): lock coupling does not scale well, even in the lookup experiment and with read-write locks (50M random 8-byte keys, 20 hyper-threads).
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper): going from 1 to 20 threads raises L1 misses significantly and CPU cycles by a factor of 6.6x; the file ties this to lock coupling.
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper), cycles per lookup at 1 thread / 20 threads: no sync 211 / 381; lock coupling 418 / 2787; OLC 348 / 418; ROWEX 375 / 427.
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper): lock coupling simply does not scale on modern multi- and many-core CPUs.
Lehman and Yao 1981: a process manipulating the tree uses only a small constant number of locks at any time, and no search is ever prevented from reading any node.
Lehman and Yao 1981: only one process may hold a page's lock at a time, and locks do not prevent other processes reading the locked page.
Lehman and Yao 1981: the search procedure does no locking of any kind.
Lehman and Yao 1981: at most three nodes are ever locked at once, and only when following a link pointer while inserting a pointer to a split node.
Lehman and Yao 1981: three nodes are locked only for the duration of one operation.
Lehman and Yao 1981: the deleter locks only one node, and deletion allows fewer than K entries in a leaf node, so nodes are not merged.
Leis and others 2016: Optimistic Lock Coupling and ROWEX scale very well with very similar performance, OLC about 7% faster for lookup (Xeon E5-2687W v3, 10 cores, 20 hyper-threads).
Leis and others 2016: single-threaded, OLC overhead against the non-synchronized variant is around 65%, and with 20 threads only 10%.
Leis and others 2016: OLC performs very well as long as there are few conflicts, but all operations may restart.
Leis and others 2016: in pathological cases a read may be restarted repeatedly, and limiting the number of optimistic restarts ensures forward progress.
Leis and others 2016 (1 lookup thread plus 1 insert-and-remove thread, 10M keys, skew up to 83% on one key): ROWEX alone keeps very high lookup performance under extreme contention.
Cervini and others (cited in Leis and others 2016): replacing fine-grained locks with elided HTM locks at the same granularity does not improve performance.
Levandoski, Lomet and Sengupta 2013 (Bw-tree): a page is never updated in place; an update prepends a delta record to the existing page.
Bw-tree 2013: the CAS on the mapping-table entry is the only physical pointer change needed to install a page update, and a failed CAS is retried.
Bw-tree 2013: consolidation is triggered when an accessor thread finds that a delta chain length has exceeded a system threshold.
Bw-tree 2013 Table I: the record update failure rate (inserts, updates, deletes) is below 0.02% for all workloads.
Bw-tree 2013 Table I: split and consolidate failures are about 1.25% on Xbox and dedup and 8.88% on synthetic.
Bw-tree 2013, Xbox workload: 10.4M operations/second against BerkeleyDB's 555K, a speedup of 18.7x.
Bw-tree 2013: speedups over BerkeleyDB are 8.6x on dedup and 5.8x on synthetic, attributed to higher latch-free failure rates.
Bw-tree 2013 outperforms the skip list by 3.7x on synthetic and by 4.4x on read-only.
Bw-tree 2013 Table II, Bw-tree against skip list: synthetic 3.83M vs 1.02M ops/sec; read-only 5.71M vs 1.30M ops/sec.
Bw-tree 2013: the Bw-tree runs at about 99% processor utilization, against about 60% for BerkeleyDB.
Wang and others 2018: an optimized Bw-tree variant achieves 1.1-2.5x better performance than the original Microsoft design for highly concurrent workloads.
note: The file's quote stops mid-sentence at the line; the rest of the sentence is not in the file.

claim: Wang and others 2018: the Bw-tree's indirection layer and delta records make it under-perform the lock-based indexes by 1.5-4.5x.
Wang and others 2018: ART is more than 4x faster than OpenBw-Tree on point lookups, and OpenBw-Tree is often 2x slower than Masstree and the B+Tree.
Wang and others 2018: the unoptimized B+Tree is 3.7x faster than OpenBw-Tree on Mono-Int insert-only.
Wang and others 2018: the B+Tree with OLC is usually 3-5x faster than all other indexes on scan and insert.
Wang and others 2018: OpenBw-Tree's higher instruction count comes from delta chain traversal, and its higher cache misses from the Mapping Table.
Wang and others 2018: the original Bw-tree's centralized epoch counter becomes a bottleneck with many threads because of cache-coherence traffic.
Wang and others 2018: removing the cache-line invalidation on the shared epoch counter (decentralized GC) gives a 1.3x improvement with 20 threads.
Wang and others 2018: Masstree has high single-threaded Mono-Int insert-only throughput but scales only 3x using 20 threads.
Wang and others 2018: the lock-free skip list showed high variation and low performance for most multi-threaded experiments.
McKenney 2001 (RCU paper): the search function contains no locks or atomic instructions, so it scales with CPU clock rate rather than memory latency.
McKenney 2001: read-intensive means update fraction f is much smaller than the reciprocal of the number of CPUs (on eight CPUs, f much less than 0.125).
McKenney 2001 (Linux 2.4.2 chat benchmark, PIII Xeon 700MHz, 1 to 4 CPUs): the RCU version attains over 30% more throughput at four CPUs.
McKenney perfbook 2023, Quick Quiz 9.59 (448 CPUs, 2.1 GHz): the question puts RCU read-side overhead at less than a 300-picosecond overhead, and the book says RCU scales quite well.
note: The 300-picosecond figure is in the quiz question, not a measured result in the file.

claim: McKenney perfbook 2023, read-only hash test: RCU beats per-bucket locking and does slightly better than hazard pointers.
McKenney perfbook 2023: RCU's non-ideal curve past 224 CPUs comes from hardware multithreading.
McKenney perfbook 2023: deferred-processing techniques such as RCU are most directly applicable to read-mostly situations, and the book asks 'But what about updates?'
McKenney perfbook 2023: update-mostly workloads requiring consistent data are rarely good places to use RCU.
McKenney 2001: a simple deletion will give good speedups only if there are many more searches than deletions.
note: The file also says writers still serialise on a lock (Figure 9, spin_lock around delete); that is the file's own gloss.

claim: Wikipedia (seqlock) summary: a seqlock beats a reader-writer lock when readers are many and writers few, fails for pointer data, and heavy writing can starve readers.
McKenney perfbook 2023: sequence locks incur the overhead of a pair of memory barriers for each attempt to execute the critical section.
Wikipedia (non-blocking algorithm), quoted: wait-free means every operation has a bound on the number of steps.
Herlihy 1991 (TOPLAS 13(1)): compare-and-swap has an infinite consensus number (textbook, not fetched).
Wikipedia (non-blocking algorithm) summary: universal constructions are slower than naive blocking designs.
Kogan-Petrank queue (2011) is about as fast as a lock-free queue (summary only).
Wang and others 2018: although the Bw-tree is lock-free, threads are not guaranteed to make progress because of failed CAS.
ABA fixes, summary only (Wikipedia): tags, hazard pointers, double-width CAS, LL/SC, and deferred free.

Dice, Shalev and Shavit 2006 (TL2): red-black trees made concurrent mechanically from sequential code with TL2 tend to perform as well as prior algorithms, comparable to hand-crafted fine-grained lock-based ones; TL2 is an order of magnitude faster than sequential code under a single lock.

Dice et al 2006 (TL2): on a 16-processor Sun V890 red-black tree (5% and 30% puts and deletes; key ranges 100-200 and 10,000-20,000), all algorithms scale quite well to 16 processors except the mutual-exclusion one.
Dice et al 2006 (TL2): Hanke's hand-crafted algorithm gives the highest throughput in most cases, because its single-thread overhead is below that of all STM algorithms.
Dice et al 2006 (TL2): Ennals's algorithm performs badly on the contended write-dominated benchmark, apparently from frequent transaction collisions.
Dice et al 2006 (TL2): the global version clock causes invalidation traffic from updates of the clock, which makes TL/PO beat TL2 on small trees.
Dice et al 2006 (TL2): in all benchmarks the STM algorithms are an order of magnitude faster than the single-lock Mutex implementation.
Cascaval and others 2008, second hand via the 2011 STM rebuttal: with real hardware STM performs worse than sequential code, on a STAMP subset and one micro-benchmark, using up to 8 threads.
note: Second hand: the 2008 paper was not read (blocked), and the words are as the 2011 rebuttal quotes them.

claim: Cascaval and others 2008, second hand via the 2011 rebuttal: in the vacation benchmark STM stops scaling at 4 threads, and genome is about 2.5x at 8 threads.
note: Second hand, as with the preceding record.

claim: 2011 STM rebuttal (SwissTM, per the file): STM outperforms sequential code by up to 29 times on SPARC with 64 threads and by up to 9 times on x86 with 16 threads.
2011 STM rebuttal: on STMBench7 write (90% write operations, very high contention) STM-ME does not beat sequential code.
2011 STM rebuttal: STM-MT outperforms sequential code by up to 23 times (STM-ME up to 29 times), and by 5.6 times on average (STM-ME 9.1 times).
note: The file reads this gap as the cost of transparent privatization.

claim: 2011 STM rebuttal: on x86, STM beats sequential code in 3 of 17 workloads with 2 threads and in 13 workloads with 4 threads.
HTM, summary from search snippets only: best-effort, needs a lock fallback, write set about 30.5 KiB, and a 2021 study found it comparable to locking.
Leis and others 2016 (ART paper): HTM insert was slowed by contention in the memory allocator, causing frequent aborts.
Bolosky and Scott 1993: the contribution of false sharing to total shared-memory cost could range from nothing to over 90% of total cost (trace simulation of 16 programs, not wall-clock).

Bolosky and Scott 1993 (quicksort, trace simulation, cost units): data-transfer cost is 1.2 billion at 8K blocks, 138 million at 1K (ratio 8.7), and 28 million at 128 bytes (43 times less than at 8K).
Bolosky and Scott 1993: the SOR application has very little false sharing, and its data-transfer cost component is never greater than 10% of total cost.
Bolosky and Scott 1993: most applications in their suite display performance like that of the quicksort, scene rendering and Cholesky programs.
Bolosky and Scott 1993 cite others: removing false sharing cut overall bus utilization by up to about 25%, for cache lines no larger than 64 bytes.
Wikipedia (False sharing) summary: 20 threads each incrementing their own byte took about 50 times more compute time than when padded to 64 bytes.
Cache-coherence snooping has a limit of about 64 processors (summary only).
McKenney perfbook 2023: with 8 CPUs incrementing one shared variable, each CPU waits at least 35 ns for each other CPU's increment before its own 5 ns increment.
Wikipedia (persistent data structure) summary: path copying costs O(log n) per update on a balanced tree; Driscoll and others 1989 get an O(1) slowdown.
Wikipedia (LSM tree) summary: a memtable is flushed as sorted runs and compacted; leveling versus tiering trades write amplification against read cost.
Log-structured writing: a single appender is the common case, and one tail lock or CAS can serve several appenders (textbook, not fetched).
Persistent path-copied trees: under concurrent writers a CAS on the root fails, and all but one writer must redo its copy (reasoning, not measured in this file).
note: The file marks this TEXTBOOK and also says it is reasoning, not measured here.
